questions.question: 'Slim', 'thin' and 'skinny' all describe low body weight. What distinguishes them, and why does word choice matter in writing?
questions.solution: They share a DENOTATION (the literal meaning: low weight) but differ in CONNOTATION (the emotional shading): 'slim' is approving, 'thin' neutral, 'skinny' disapproving. Word choice controls the reader's attitude without changing the literal fact — connotation is where tone, bias and persuasion live. Choose words for both layers.

questions.question: You meet an unknown word 'gregarious' in 'He was so gregarious that he organised a gathering every weekend.' Which context-clue type is at work, and name the other types.
questions.solution: This is an EXAMPLE/EXPLANATION clue — the rest of the sentence demonstrates the meaning (sociable, fond of company). Other types: DEFINITION (the word is directly defined), SYNONYM/RESTATEMENT (a familiar word repeats the idea), CONTRAST/ANTONYM (a signal like 'but' or 'unlike' points the opposite way). Skilled readers combine all four rather than stopping at a dictionary.

questions.concept: Prefix and suffix as meaning machines
questions.question: Without a dictionary, work out the meaning of 'misinterpretation' and 'unbelievable' using word parts.
questions.solution: 'mis-' (wrongly) + 'interpret' (explain meaning) + '-ation' (the act/result) → a wrong explanation of something's meaning. 'un-' (not) + 'believe' + '-able' (capable of) → not able to be believed. Prefixes modify meaning, roots carry the core, suffixes set the word class — decomposing unfamiliar vocabulary is faster and more reliable than guessing from context alone.

questions.question: Rewrite 'The kids got a load of cool stuff for Xmas' in formal register, and state what actually changed.
questions.solution: 'The children received many gifts at Christmas.' Changed: contraction removed, slang ('kids', 'a load of', 'cool') replaced by neutral equivalents, colloquial abbreviation ('Xmas') standardised. Register is the match between language and situation — formal writing needs full forms, precise vocabulary and no slang, while informal writing trades those for warmth and speed.

questions.concept: Collocation — why some pairs sound right
questions.question: Why do we say 'heavy rain' but not 'strong rain', and 'strong tea' but not 'heavy tea'? What is collocation?
questions.solution: Collocation is the conventional pairing of words that native usage has fixed: 'heavy' pairs with rain, traffic, smoker; 'strong' with tea, coffee, argument. Neither dictionary definition forbids the other pair — usage alone does. Learning words in their common partnerships (not in isolation) is what makes output sound natural rather than translated.

questions.question: 'Big', 'large', 'huge' and 'vast' are all synonyms of size. Why can't they be swapped freely in every sentence?
questions.solution: They differ in REGISTER (formal/informal), INTENSITY (huge > big) and COLLOCATIONAL RANGE (vast fits deserts and oceans, not people). Substituting changes tone and sometimes idiomatic correctness ('a vast man' sounds wrong). Synonyms form a spectrum of degree and appropriateness — precision in writing comes from choosing the exact point on that spectrum.

questions.question: Why can't you understand 'to kick the bucket' by adding up the meanings of its words, and how should a learner handle idioms?
questions.solution: An idiom is a FIXED expression whose meaning is attached to the whole phrase, not the individual words — 'kick the bucket' means 'to die', though no kicking or bucket is involved. Learners must treat idioms as single vocabulary items: learn the meaning, the typical contexts and any grammatical rigidity ('kick the bucket' cannot become 'kick the pail').

questions.question: You have 5 minutes to (a) decide whether an article is worth reading and (b) find the year a bridge was built. Which strategy fits each task, and what is the difference?
questions.solution: (a) SKIMMING: read titles, first/last sentences of paragraphs to grasp the gist — a fast pass for overall meaning. (b) SCANNING: move your eyes over the text hunting for the specific item (a year, a name) without reading everything. Skimming takes the shape of the text; scanning targets a datum. Choosing the right strategy for the purpose is the core reading skill.
